    AI Overview
    Hydrocodone is
    a potent opioid analgesic used to treat severe pain, often combined with acetaminophen (e.g., Vicodin, Norco). It functions by altering the central nervous system's response to pain. Due to high addiction risk, it is a controlled substance often abused, leading to physical dependence, severe withdrawal symptoms, and potential overdose. 
    Key Aspects of Hydrocodone Use: 
    • Medical Uses: It is prescribed for moderate to severe pain and sometimes as a cough suppressant.
    • Side Effects: Common side effects include constipation, dizziness, drowsiness, dry mouth, nausea, and vomiting.
    • Warnings & Risks:
      It has high potential for addiction, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death. Long-term use can cause physical dependence and adrenal insufficiency.
    • Withdrawal Symptoms: Stopping suddenly can trigger withdrawal symptoms, which may include restlessness, muscle pain, anxiety, and insomnia.
    • Drug Interactions: Alcohol, other opioids, and certain antidepressants should be avoided as they can increase the risk of severe drowsiness, respiratory depression, and death. 
    Important Safety Information
    Do not take this medication without a prescription, and never take more than prescribed. Always inform your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. 
    Disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Consult a healthcare professional for diagnosis and treatment.

    AI Overview
    Hydrocodone is a semisynthetic opioid synthesized in Germany in 1920 from codeine or thebaine by Carl Mannich and Helene Löwenheim, approved by the FDA in 1943 for pain and cough suppression. Originally marketed as Hycodan, it was rescheduled from Schedule III to Schedule II in 2014 to combat widespread abuse and addiction. 
    Key Historical Milestones 
    • 1920: First synthesized in Germany.
    • 1923: First reports suggesting it causes euphoria and habituation.
    • 1943: Approved for sale in the U.S. by the FDA.
    • 1961: First official reports of dependency and addiction published.
    • 1998: Approval of many common combinations with acetaminophen.
    • 2014: Reclassified by the DEA as a Schedule II controlled substance, tightening controls.
    Synonyms and Common Trade Names
    Historically, this drug has been known by several synonyms, including: 
    Dihydrocodeinone, Vicodin, Lortab, Norco, Hycodan, and Vicoprofen.
    Usage Examples & Trends
    • Pain Relief: Known as an oral semi-synthetic mu-opioid receptor agonist commonly used for moderate to severe pain. 
    • Antitussive: Used in combined forms for its ability to suppress coughs. 
    • Prescription Trends: Often paired with acetaminophen, it became one of the most widely prescribed painkillers in the US before strict controls, with prescriptions declining from over 68 million in 2014 to around 30 million in the early 2020s.

      How it Works. What is the mechanism of action of hydrocodone?

      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Hydrocodone is a semisynthetic opioid agonist that acts primarily as a mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonist within the central nervous system, with some action on kappa (
      κkappa
      )       receptors.             By binding to these receptors, it inhibits the release of neurotransmitters, reduces neuronal excitability, alters pain perception, and increases pain threshold, causing analgesia, sedation, and a decreased cough reflex. 
      Key Aspects of Hydrocodone Mechanism of Action:
      • Synonyms/Related Processes:
        Opioid agonist, CNS depressant, mu-opiate receptor modulator. 
      • Action on Pain Pathways:
        It inhibits ascending pain pathways in the central nervous system, causing inhibition of neurotransmitter release (e.g., substance P). 
      • Active Metabolite:
        While a weak agonist on its own, hydrocodone is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) enzyme to hydromorphone, a much more potent opioid receptor agonist. 
      • Onset and Duration:
        It acts within 10–15 minutes, with peak effects in 30–60 minutes, lasting 3–6 hours. 
      • Usage Examples:
        It is primarily used for the management of severe, acute, or chronic pain that cannot be treated with nonopioid alternatives, as well as an antitussive for nonproductive coughs. 
      Hydrocodone also acts on the brain's reward pathway by inhibiting neurons in the ventral tegmental area. It is important to note that it is a Schedule II controlled substance due to high abuse potential.

        AI Overview
        Hydrocodone (
        C18H21NO3cap C sub 18 cap H sub 21 cap N cap O sub 3
        )         is a semi-synthetic opioid related to codeine, with the chemical name 4,5α-epoxy-3-methoxy-17-methylmorphinan-6-one.                 It is a morphinan derivative featuring an epoxide bridge, a methyl ether, and a ketone group (dihydrocodeinone), structurally characterized by its analgesic properties and controlled-substance status. 
        Key Structural Information:
        • Molecular Formula:
          C18H21NO3cap C sub 18 cap H sub 21 cap N cap O sub 3
           
        • Molecular Weight:
          299.4 g/mol299.4 g/mol
           
        • IUPAC Name: (4R,4aR,7aR,12bS)-9-methoxy-3-methyl-1,2,4,4a,5,6,7a,13-octahydro-4,12-methanobenzofuro[3,2-e]isoquinolin-7-one 
        • CAS Number: 125-29-1 (base) 
        • Structure Components: A saturated ring system (dihydro-) compared to codeine, with a ketone at position 6, a methoxy group at position 3, and an N-methyl group. 
        Hydrocodone is often used in medicine as a bitartrate salt (
        C18H21NO3⋅C4H6O6cap C sub 18 cap H sub 21 cap N cap O sub 3 center dot cap C sub 4 cap H sub 6 cap O sub 6
        )        , frequently combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen.

          Drug Interactions. What are the drug interactions of hydrocodone?
          Feedback
          More seriously, hydrocodone can increase your risk of slowed breathing, overdose, and death. Other hydrocodone interactions include antidepressants like fluoxetine (Prozac) and diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide (Microzide). Seizure medications like carbamazepine (Tegretol) can also interact.May 10, 2024
